name: Heat transfer
seoTitle: Heat transfer Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Heat transfer: work out mass (M) from the specific heat and the initial temperature. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the specific heat, the initial temperature, the final temperature and the thermal conductivity and the Heat transfer calculator solves for mass (M). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The results leave the screen the moment you edit a field; press Calculate and they come back updated, so a single changed input shows its own effect.

sections.title: How does the Heat transfer calculator work?
sections.html:
The Heat transfer calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mass (M) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the I want to calculate); then you type in the specific heat (C), the initial temperature (T1), the final temperature (T2) and the thermal conductivity (K).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Heat transfer calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mass (M)=-1000 × heat transfer (Q) ÷ (specific heat (C) × (initial temperature (T1) − final temperature (T2)))
Cross sectional area (A)=-heat transfer (Q) × thickness of material (l) ÷ (thermal conductivity (K) × time taken (t) × (cold temperature (Tc) − hot temperature (Th)))
Heat transferred per unit time (Q)=surface area (A) × convective heat transfer coefficient (Hc) × (-bulk temperature (T1) + surface temperature (T2))
Area of hot object (A)=-100000000000000 ÷ 5670367 × radiative heat transfer per unit time (Q) ÷ (emissivity (e) × ((temperature of object (T1) ^ 4) − (temperature of environment (T2) ^ 4)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Specific heat capacity, opening in joules per kilogram per kelvin
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Thermal conductivity, opening in watts per meter-kelvin
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Heat transfer calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the specific heat, the initial temperature and the final temperature — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Heat transfer calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mass (M), derived from the specific heat, the initial temperature and the final temperature. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Heat transfer calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the specific heat, the initial temperature, the final temperature and the thermal conductivity, which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass (M) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass (M) opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Heat transfer calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
